material-work.text: Pottery manufacture and food procurement combined practical skills with local resources and some moved materials. Shared decoration, material origin and the work of provisioning require different evidence.

evidence.text: Dated pottery, settlement remains and food evidence must be considered together; a design alone cannot recover an entire voyage.

production.text: Ceramic technique and seafaring knowledge supported communities whose subsistence strategies could differ.

name: Lapita: pottery and island voyaging
place: Bismarck Archipelago and routes into Remote Oceania
geographicPrecision: Broad emergence region; not one exact starting village or a territorial border.

interval.label: c. 1500–500 BCE
interval.note: Broad pottery-style frame in the museum essay; regional settlement and later histories have different dates.

question: What work turned a sea crossing into a lasting island community?
summary: Potters, navigators and food producers helped establish communities across different island environments. Stamped designs, raw materials, dated tools and food evidence reveal different parts of that work. Their histories continued when decorated pottery changed; a shared pattern is a starting point for investigation, rather than a recovered voyage.

sections.title: A repeated mark became a larger design
sections.text: Lapita decoration began with practical actions. A potter pressed a toothed tool into clay before firing, combining small impressions into repeated bands and more elaborate figures. The Met describes vessels that may have cooked, served or stored food. Making such an object joined a useful container with choices about its surface. Repetition required control of spacing and direction: a pattern was something a maker constructed, rather than a label that appeared automatically on every pot.

citations.locator: Ceramic technique and proposed vessel uses

sections.title: Settlement joined voyaging with provisioning
sections.text: Irwin’s regional account places the Lapita complex in the Bismarck Archipelago around 1500 BCE and movement toward Fiji and West Polynesia especially around 1100–800 BCE. These were different communities and stages, not one arrival everywhere. Coastal settings offered access to boats and marine resources. Transporting useful plants and animals could help establish livelihoods, while catching and gathering food sustained people locally. The timing and combination differed: the earliest eastern communities cannot simply be assigned an identical, fully established farming package.

citations.locator: Emergence; Lapita in Remote Oceania; transported foods and differing subsistence interpretations

sections.title: Potters also worked with local materials
sections.text: A shared decorative tradition did not require every vessel to arrive by canoe. Dickinson and Nunn examined sand temper in pottery from Fiji’s Rove Peninsula. Most sampled sherds used related local sands; a few contained nonlocal volcanic material. The authors interpret the latter as ceramic transfer. Distinguish that interpretation from the observed temper: identifying nonlocal material does not by itself rule out movement of raw ingredients or name a carrier. Looking inside the fabric changes the question from whether two designs resemble each other to how particular materials and finished objects may have moved.

citations.locator: Published abstract: local temper groups and three nonlocal sherds

sections.title: Meals made an island habitable
sections.text: At Teouma on Efate, researchers investigated dietary protein through bone-collagen isotopes and local food baselines. Their interpretation combines reef and inshore resources, wild terrestrial animals and domestic animals. This makes food acquisition and animal care part of settlement history, alongside navigation. It does not supply a complete menu: low-protein plant foods can be less visible in this kind of measurement. The study concerns one early Vanuatu community and must retain that setting when compared with other islands.

citations.locator: Abstract; Stable isotope analysis and paleodietary reconstruction; Conclusions

sections.title: Changing pottery did not end community history
sections.text: Tonga’s sequence shows why the pottery frame needs a longer context. Decorated vessels gave way to plain forms, while settlements occupied a wider range of places, including island interiors. A 2018 study argues that local ceramic production had ceased by about 2350 calibrated years before 1950, approximately 400 BCE. That estimate falls after this dossier’s 500 BCE endpoint. It marks a proposed change in material practice, not the disappearance of islanders or a universal stage that every Pacific society had to follow.

deeperReading.title: A dated tool is not a dated voyage
deeperReading.text: At Nukuleka, researchers dated Acropora coral files using uranium–thorium measurements. A sample from beach sand below a midden helped position early occupation near 890 BCE. The argument connects material, use and stratigraphic context; it does not date a ship’s departure. The study screened for alteration, and some dates were rejected. Samples redeposited in a later mound cannot be treated as if they remained in their original occupation layer.

citations.locator: Sample Context; Materials and Methods; Results: Strata II–IV

deeperReading.title: An island sequence has overlapping uncertainties
deeperReading.text: The 2015 Tongan analysis combined different dated materials and modeled the principal island groups separately. Its estimates placed expansion beyond Tongatapu within succeeding generations, while the first-settlement ranges for Ha’apai and Vava’u overlapped. Limited Vava’u samples constrained the proposed order. A useful timeline therefore displays an attributed model and uncertainty, rather than turning three named islands into an exact recovered itinerary for one crew.

deeperReading.title: Pottery and language answer related questions differently
deeperReading.text: Pawley argues for connections between Lapita archaeology and Oceanic language history through distributions, shared linguistic innovations and material terminology. He also notes that pottery could enter communities speaking other languages. A sherd does not record its maker’s speech. Keep the linguistic argument visible as a reconstruction, rather than use a decorative style as an ethnic badge or an automatic identification of every person who handled it.

deeperReading.title: Follow a mechanism across the comparison
deeperReading.text: Compare how a community obtained useful materials, supplied meals and renewed practical skills. Those questions connect this case with the other coastal inquiries without turning their different histories into one route. For each answer, name the evidence that makes the proposed work visible.

evidenceReading.title: Materials, dates and food need different readings
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of the selected studies, not ancient quotations. Match the inference to the material and context actually examined.

items.label: Observed temper and interpreted transfer
items.text: The Rove abstract identifies mostly local temper and a few sherds containing nonlocal volcanic material. Its authors interpret the latter as transfer of pottery.
items.interpretation: Keep the interpretation attributed. Material identification alone neither names a carrier nor rules out movement of raw ingredients; a decorative resemblance is a different observation.

items.label: A coral tool in a deposit
items.text: The Nukuleka study used uranium–thorium measurements on coral files, screened alteration and distinguished primary occupation deposits from redeposited mound fill.
items.interpretation: An associated tool and its deposition help position settlement. This is not an exact departure date, the age of every sherd or a record of one sailing course.

items.label: Protein sources rather than every meal
items.text: The Teouma study analyzed forty-nine adults against food baselines and declined exact dietary percentages.
items.interpretation: The result investigates dietary protein in this community. It is not a complete menu, an individual recipe or an identical provisioning system for every island.

familyActivity.title: Make a repeat; investigate a connection
steps: Read the first section’s description of toothed stamping. An adult can read it aloud. Draw your own small three-mark shape.
Repeat your mark across a paper band. Change its spacing or direction, then explain how the small actions make a larger pattern.
Read the Rove material-study paraphrase. Name evidence needed before using two actual pottery finds to investigate movement between places.
familyActivity.explanation: Your paper band demonstrates a possible making action, not a recovered ancient motif or tool. The supplied account describes a technique; dated archaeological contexts and material study support different questions about movement. No particular voyage is reconstructed.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded manufacturing, provisioning and island-sequence account; main/deeper/evidence reading, text-supplied family inquiry and separate phased context. The entire original case interval, object IDs, dimensions and claims remain; no media or historical relation is added by this module.
limitations: The complete c. 1500–500 BCE case interval remains untouched, including its existing note and precision. The separate context extends to a later attributed Tongan ceramic boundary.

Rove consultation is limited to the published abstract and metadata; the article body and appendix were not read. Ceramic transfer is the authors’ interpretation rather than an automatic conclusion from nonlocal temper.

Selected publisher HTML sections support the chronological and dietary accounts. Supplementary individual tables and models were not reanalyzed; older calibration choices and differing probability levels remain part of the studies.
The isotope study concerns dietary protein in forty-nine Teouma adults. No complete menu, exact diet percentages, universal island subsistence or fixed gendered work roles inferred.
Linguistic reconstruction, pottery classification and contemporary identities remain distinct. No sherd is treated as a transcript of its user’s speech.
No exact voyage, named crew, boat reconstruction, original motif meaning, complete governing system or single cause of ceramic cessation established.

placeStudy.title: Different island settings across the Pacific
placeStudy.description: This regional locator diagram crosses the 180° meridian. Three coarse island settings orient different sources; they are not one recovered canoe journey or a set of exact excavation positions. No shoreline, route, political territory or claim of the same community on every island is drawn. Rove and Nukuleka remain named research settings without invented site coordinates.

points.label: Bismarck Archipelago — broad regional orientation
points.text: The inherited broad regional anchor orients Irwin’s approximate 1500 BCE account. It does not identify a single starting village, recovered departure point or shared first arrival on every island.

points.label: Efate — Teouma study’s island setting
points.text: A coarse island point read from the study map’s graticule, accurate only at tens-of-kilometres scale. It is not the cemetery’s GPS position or an access locator. The dietary-protein study concerns Teouma’s selected early community, not every Pacific island.
